tagline: How 1:1, 1:M and M:M relationships shape filtering, performance, and model design

slides.title: What Is Cardinality?
slides.body: Cardinality defines how many rows on one side of a relationship match rows on the other side. Power BI supports three types: one-to-one (1:1), one-to-many (1:M), and many-to-many (M:M). Getting cardinality right is fundamental — wrong cardinality causes incorrect calculations, security gaps, and poor performance.
slides.keyPoint: Always prefer 1:M (star schema). 1:1 for extended attribute tables. M:M only when unavoidable — and usually requires a bridge table or specific Power BI M:M support.

slides.title: The Blank Row Problem — Referential Integrity
bullets: When a fact table contains a foreign key that has NO matching primary key in the dimension, Power BI adds a virtual blank row to the dimension to catch these orphaned fact rows.
Example: FactSales contains ProductID=999 but DimProduct has no row with ProductID=999.
Power BI adds a blank DimProduct row and assigns all orphaned sales to it.
This causes VALUES(DimProduct[ProductName]) to include a blank — often surprising in reports.
Fix: clean the data in Power Query (remove orphaned fact rows or add a placeholder dimension row), or ensure referential integrity in the source system.

slides.title: Role-Playing Dimensions — One Dimension, Multiple Relationships
slides.caption: DimDate used as OrderDate AND ShipDate in FactOrders

slides.title: Activating Inactive Relationships with USERELATIONSHIP
slides.caption: Calculate revenue by ship date using the inactive relationship
slides.expression:
Revenue by Ship Date =
    CALCULATE(
        [Total Revenue],
        USERELATIONSHIP(
            FactOrders[ShipDateID],
            DimDate[DateID]
        )
    )

-- USERELATIONSHIP deactivates the default (OrderDate)
-- relationship and activates ShipDate for this calculation only
slides.explanation: Only ONE relationship between any two tables can be active at a time. USERELATIONSHIP() lets you temporarily swap which relationship is used inside a CALCULATE expression, without changing the model permanently.

slides.title: Many-to-Many — The Risky Pattern
bullets: True M:M between two fact tables (e.g., FactSales and FactBudget with overlapping dimension keys) cannot be related directly without ambiguity.
The standard solution is a bridge (junction) table: FactA (M) → Bridge (1) → FactB (M).
Power BI's native M:M cardinality type is designed for the shared dimension pattern (e.g., DimDate used by two separate fact tables in a composite model) — NOT for fact-to-fact joins.
M:M with bidirectional cross-filtering can cause RLS bypass: filters propagate through the fact table unexpectedly, potentially exposing data to unauthorized users.
Performance impact: M:M relationships prevent VertiPaq from building efficient join indexes — query plan complexity increases significantly.

slides.title: PL-300 Exam Key Points
bullets: Always set the '1' side on the dimension table and the 'many' side on the fact table when creating relationships.
If two tables have no shared unique key, you need a bridge table — do NOT create a direct M:M without a bridge.
High cardinality columns (many distinct values — e.g., GUID or email addresses) as relationship keys reduce VertiPaq compression. Use integer surrogate keys instead.
Cross-filter direction 'Both' doubles query plan complexity and can break row-level security. Only enable it when explicitly required.
Circular relationships (A → B → C → A) are not allowed. Power BI will disable one relationship automatically and show it in grey.
